title: Context Slipstream Benchmark — scratch notebook
content:
Purpose:
- Quick personal log: explore how KV/cache reuse (shared prefixes) interacts with bursty arrival patterns when requests partially overlap in context. Looking for root cause of sporadic tail spikes during moderate bursts.

Hypothesis:
- High prefix overlap should improve per-token throughput by increasing KV hits, but multiplexing mixed-length requests causes cache churn and occasional eviction-induced stalls. Small windows of eviction cause large p99 increases.

Environment (notes):
- Cluster: 8x A100-40GB (dedicated local pool emulation)
- Model: rw-v1-13B-q4 (quantized float-like path)
- Runtime branch: context-slipstream-experiment (sha: 9f3b2d1) PR linked above
- Serving config: continuous batching ON, max_batch_size=32, batch_timeout_ms=8, kv_cache_size_shard=2GB, eviction=LRU (baseline)
- Load generator: local wrk-like harness (tools/load_test.py), 12 workers, concurrency 8

Test plan:
- Mixed-arrival profile: steady 50 qps + periodic micro-bursts (200 qps for 3s every 60s) for 30m run
- Request mix: 70% short (prompt len ~64 tokens), 30% long (prompt len ~512 tokens)
- Prefix overlap: simulate 80% prefix share in long requests (same system prompt + partial conversation reuse)
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end), per-token latency, kv_hit_rate, batch_size histogram, gRPC stall counts, GPU util, context eviction events

Quick command used: 
- python tools/load_test.py --profile slipstream --duration 1800 --workers 12 --steady-qps 50 --burst-qps 200 --burst-duration 3 --burst-interval 60 --overlap 0.8

Representative results (aggregated):
- overall throughput (stable): ~52 qps (steady), peaks to ~210 qps during bursts
- avg batch size: 18 (steady) -> 22 (burst)
- kv cache hit rate: 0.92 (steady) -> 0.67 (during bursts)
- p50 end-to-end: 42 ms (steady) -> 48 ms (burst)
- p95 end-to-end: 120 ms (steady) -> 210 ms (burst)
- p99 end-to-end: 260 ms (steady) -> 980 ms (burst, spikes observed)
- tail events: burst-correlated spikes; many p99 samples clustered inside the 3-6s after burst start

Small ascii timeline (sample run):
- t=00:00 steady 50qps, p99~260ms, kv_hit~0.92
- t=05:12 burst start, qps->200, within 1s kv_hit drops to 0.7, p99 jumps to 720ms
- t=05:15 additional long requests overlap => eviction events logged, gRPC stall count +3
- t=05:24 recovery begins, kv_hit climbs back, p99 returns toward baseline by t=05:36 (~12s after burst start)

Observations / diagnostics:
- Eviction pattern: when many long requests hit concurrently, the shard-level KV cache shows LRU churn. Long requests reuse large prefix ranges causing short requests to evict chunks needed by still-running long requests -> cache miss cascade.
- Batching interaction: larger batches during peaks amplify side-effects: a single cache miss in a batch affects many tokens.
- gRPC stalls: correlated with the moments when controller switched to fallback kernel because cache miss caused KV fetch to block on I/O (observed 50–150ms stalls).
- Recovery: once burst subsides, cache warms back in ~8–14s depending on long-request fraction.

Quick conclusions / mitigations to try (prioritized):
1) Pre-warm strategy: keep a tiny pre-warmed set of popular prefixes pinned to avoid eviction on mid-sized bursts (cheap memory reservation).
2) Segment-aware eviction: switch from plain LRU to segment-aware (prefer to evict cold short-token segments rather than contiguous long-prefixs).
3) Soft-priority lane: route suspected cache-sensitive requests into a low-concurrency lane to reduce cross-eviction pressure.
4) Batch timeout tuning: lower batch_timeout_ms from 8 -> 4ms during detected bursts (tradeoff: more small batches but fewer massive simultaneous misses).
5) Instrument per-request prefix cardinality to detect which conversations are heavy-cache consumers and optionally limit concurrency per conversation.

Next runs (planned):
- A: segment-aware eviction prototype (patch locally) + identical slipstream profile, measure p99 improvement
- B: pre-warm reserved slot test (reserve 10% of shard kv cache)
- C: dynamic batch_timeout experiment (auto-scale batch timeout downward on burst detection)
- D: replay real production traces (sample) for 1h to validate lab replicability

Notes for follow-up / ad-hoc items:
- Check PR 1549 for kernel changes that reduce I/O blocking on cache miss (might already reduce stall times)
- Add event trace IDs to load generator for easier correlation (TODO in tools/load_test.py)
- Capture and save one full binary trace for the large spike (file saved under /tmp/context-slipstream-traces/run-20250114-0512.trace)

Questions left open:
- Is LRU always the wrong default for mixed-length contexts? Might be OK for long-tail workloads, but mixed-length workloads seem to benefit from topology-aware eviction.
- How often do real users create these high-overlap long-requests in prod vs our synthetic workload? Next: sample production metadata (safe, no PII) and run replay.

Immediate TODOs (me):
- Push segment-eviction prototype branch and run job A (target 2025-02-04)
- Add per-request prefix-cardinality histogram to tracing agent (small change)
- Sync with Miguel (cache policy) and Leah (batching heuristics) next Thurs

Bottom line (scratch): slipstream-style bursts with high prefix overlap produce pronounced, short-lived p99 spikes driven by KV cache eviction cascades. Fixes likely in caching policy + conservative laneing / timeout heuristics rather than large infra changes.

End.
